title: The letters of the New Testament
tagline: Twenty-one letters, written to real churches and friends, dictated, signed, carried by hand, read aloud, copied and gathered, until they became more than a third of the New Testament.

intro.text: Twenty-one of the New Testament's twenty-seven books are letters: thirteen that open with Paul's name, the unsigned "word of exhortation" to the Hebrews, and seven shorter letters under the names of James, Peter, John and Jude. Counted in the site's King James text, they fill 2,767 of the New Testament's 7,957 verses (about 35 per cent) and 121 of its 260 chapters.

They were written to people in real places: the churches of Rome, Corinth and Thessalonica, believers scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor, a householder named Philemon, "the wellbeloved Gaius". Their writers would rather have come in person and spoken "face to face"; a letter, written "with paper and ink", stood in for the visit. Paul, at least, usually dictated to a secretary and closed in his own hand.

Acts tells the story that many of the letters fit into: the founding of the churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus, and the travels of Silas, Timothy, Apollos, Aquila and Priscilla, who all reappear in the letters. The letters in turn take the Gospel story for granted, as Schaff observes: Christ's death and resurrection, the Lord's Supper "received of the Lord", and the voice heard on "the holy mount". Deissmann thought Luke wrote Acts without knowing Paul's letters, which were written but not yet gathered.

This study follows the order of the English Bible, which comes from the Latin Vulgate, and groups the letters in four: Paul's thirteen; Hebrews, which names no author; James, Peter and Jude; and the three letters of John. The last two groups make up the seven letters the early church called "catholic", meaning general: Eusebius, about 325, already speaks of "the seven so-called catholic epistles".

claim.text: An ancient letter began with one formula: the sender's name, the reader's name, and a greeting. "Apion to Epimachus his father and lord, many greetings," wrote a young Egyptian soldier in the second century. James and the Jerusalem letter in Acts keep the plain Greek word for "greeting" (chairein); Paul and Peter enlarge every part, naming the sender's calling and describing the readers, and turn the greeting into a blessing: "Grace to you and peace." The address itself, Deissmann notes, was written on the outside of the folded sheet, and none of the New Testament letters preserves it.

Next came a wish for the reader's health and thanks to the gods: Apion thanks "the lord Serapis" for saving him at sea, and countless papyrus letters assure the reader of the writer's prayers. Paul turns this courtesy into thanksgiving to God and prayer for his readers in almost every letter, and 3 John keeps the old health-wish nearly word for word: "I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health." Galatians has no thanksgiving at all; it moves straight to "I marvel that ye are so soon removed".

letterForm.part: Body: the business of the letter

claim.text: Papyrus writers moved into their business with set phrases such as "I would have you know", and Paul uses the same signals: "I would ye should understand", "I would not have you ignorant", or "Now concerning" to take up a question his readers had sent him. Schaff calls this part the letters' "doctrinal expositions". It may run to a few sentences, as in Philemon, or to many chapters, as in Romans.

Most letters turn from teaching to what Schaff calls "practical exhortations and consolations", often at a hinge such as "I beseech you therefore". Some of this is the common language of letters too: Deissmann thought "comfort one another with these words" was taken from the closing advice of ancient letters of consolation. Hebrews calls itself, as a whole, "the word of exhortation".

Near the end come greetings, sent to named friends and passed on from others. "The writers of papyrus letters often commission greetings to various persons, and often convey them from others, just as St. Paul does in most of his letters" (Deissmann). Romans 16 greets about two dozen people by name; Hebrews passes on greetings from "they of Italy", 1 Peter from "Marcus my son", and 3 John asks Gaius to "greet the friends by name".

A letter written out by a secretary was often finished in the sender's own hand, and that closing line proved it genuine. Paul mentions doing so five times and calls his greeting "the token in every epistle". Deissmann, comparing papyrus letters whose last lines are in a second hand, argued that Paul signed all his letters this way even where he does not say so; Lightfoot saw the practice as a precaution against forgeries.

Ancient letters closed with a short farewell: "Fare thee well, I pray," Apion signs off. The Jerusalem letter in Acts ends "Fare ye well", and 2 Corinthians keeps a "Finally, brethren, farewell". But the New Testament letters characteristically end with a blessing of grace, or, in Hebrews, 2 Peter and Jude, with a short hymn of praise to God.

hands.name: Tertius
hands.note: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle": the only secretary named in Paul's letters. Conybeare and Howson guessed from his Latin name that he was a Roman Christian.

hands.name: Silvanus (one reading)
hands.note: "By Silvanus ... I have written briefly": Bigg reads him as the secretary who shaped the Greek; Moorehead (ISBE) as the bearer. The words allow either.

hands.name: Paul, in his own hand
hands.note: "The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand."

hands.name: Paul, in his own hand
hands.note: "How large a letter I have written": Lightfoot reads the Greek as "in what large letters", the big strokes of Paul's own hand after the secretary's.

hands.name: Paul, in his own hand
hands.note: "The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds."

hands.name: Paul, in his own hand
hands.note: "Which is the token in every epistle: so I write."

hands.name: Paul, in his own hand
hands.note: A signed promise: "I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it."

hands.name: Phebe
hands.note: Commended as "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea"; Conybeare and Howson take her to be the bearer. The KJV's old closing note "sent by Phebe" says the same, but it is a later addition, not Scripture.

hands.name: Tychicus
hands.note: Sent "for the same purpose" in nearly the same words as in Colossians.

hands.name: Tychicus
hands.note: Lightfoot calls him "the personal link of connexion" between Ephesians and Colossians.

hands.name: Onesimus
hands.note: Travels with Tychicus, "a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you".

hands.name: Onesimus
hands.note: "Whom I have sent again": the subject of the letter goes home with it.

hands.name: Epaphroditus
hands.note: The Philippians' messenger, sent back to them; the ancient Latin prologue says Paul wrote "by Epaphroditus".

hands.name: Titus
hands.note: Sent to Corinth with two brothers. The KJV's closing note names him and Luke as bearers; that note is a later addition, not Scripture.

hands.name: Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus
hands.note: Visitors from Corinth whom Shaw (ISBE) thinks the probable bearers of the Corinthians' own letter to Paul.

hands.name: Silvanus (other reading)
hands.note: Moorehead (ISBE): "The statement denotes rather the bearer than the writer or secretary."

hands.name: Demetrius
hands.note: Vouched for by the elder; Law (ISBE) and Plummer think he probably carried the letter.

hands.name: Sosthenes
hands.note: "Sosthenes our brother". Many identify him with the synagogue ruler of Acts 18:17; neither text says so.

hands.name: Silvanus and Timothy
hands.note: "Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus": the letter speaks mostly as "we".

hands.name: Silvanus and Timothy
hands.note: The same three senders as 1 Thessalonians.

hands.name: "All the brethren which are with me"
hands.note: Unnamed companions join Paul in sending Galatians.

claim.text: 2 Peter calls Paul "our beloved brother", knows "all his epistles", finds "some things hard to be understood" in them, and sets them beside "the other scriptures". It is the only place where one group of letters speaks of another, and the earliest hint of Paul's letters read as a set; how early depends on the date of 2 Peter, which is disputed (Zahn about 60-63, Chase about 150).

"This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you." Read most simply, the first is 1 Peter. Zahn, as Bigg reports, thought it an earlier letter now lost; Mayor held that 2 Peter was not sent to the readers of 1 Peter at all.

Paul tells Colossae to have its letter read at Laodicea and to "read the epistle from Laodicea". Lightfoot sorts the old answers: a letter the Laodiceans wrote; a letter written from Laodicea (1 Timothy, say); or a letter to Laodicea, lost, or forged later, or Ephesians sent round as a circular, which was his own view. The Muratorian list already rejects a forged letter "to the Laodiceans".

letterLinks.label: "I wrote unto you in an epistle"

claim.text: "I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators": a letter before 1 Corinthians, now lost. Shaw (ISBE) suggests that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 may preserve "a stray fragment" of it.

letterLinks.label: "The things whereof ye wrote unto me"

claim.text: The traffic ran both ways: the Corinthians had written to Paul, and 1 Corinthians answers them, taking up topic after topic with "Now concerning". Shaw thinks Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus brought the church's letter.

Paul recalls a letter written "out of much affliction and anguish of heart ... with many tears" that made them sorry. Easton took it to be 1 Corinthians; Shaw (ISBE) treats it as a separate "severe letter", and reports the view, from Hausrath (1870) on, that it survives as 2 Corinthians 10-13.
Paul quotes what his critics said of his letters: "weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak". Schaff counts this among the signs that Paul wrote more letters than survive.

"Need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you?" Letters introducing a traveller were common; Deissmann prints papyrus examples and points to Romans 16, which opens "I commend unto you Phebe", as Paul's own use of the form.

The Thessalonians were not to be shaken "by letter as from us", which may mean a forged letter or a misreading of a real one; the verse does not say which. The letter closes with Paul's own hand as "the token in every epistle", a safeguard Lightfoot connects with such forgeries.

"Hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle": 2 Thessalonians points back to a letter the church already had. The only earlier letter of Paul to Thessalonica that survives is 1 Thessalonians, and Easton reads the second letter as correcting a misunderstanding of the first.

letterLinks.label: "As I wrote afore in few words"

claim.text: "As I wrote afore in few words": Schaff and Pratt (ISBE) count this among the traces of letters that have not survived. The verse itself does not say whether it means another letter or the earlier part of Ephesians.

The elder had written to Gaius's church, but Diotrephes "receiveth us not". Zahn, Schmiedel and Findlay identified that letter with 2 John; Harnack, Brooke and Law (ISBE) did not, since the two letters face different problems.

1 John says "I write unto you" four times and then "I have written unto you" twice (the Revised Version reads three and three). Plummer lists seven explanations: the second refers to the Gospel of John, which he thought most likely; to a lost earlier letter, for which "we have no evidence whatever"; to the first part of 1 John; and others, including the letter-writer's habit of looking at the letter from the reader's side.

letterLinks.to: A letter Jude meant to write
letterLinks.label: "Of the common salvation"

claim.text: Jude had set out to write "of the common salvation" but found it "needful" to write instead an appeal to "contend for the faith": a glimpse of one letter put aside for another.

Thirteen letters open with his name. Outside them, 2 Peter calls him "our beloved brother Paul" and knows "all his epistles". Eusebius counted Hebrews as Paul's fourteenth letter, noting that the church of Rome disputed it; Hebrews itself never names its writer.

Paul calls him by his Aramaic name, Cephas ("a stone"), or Peter. Paul stayed fifteen days with him, names him first among the witnesses of the risen Christ, counts him one of the three "pillars", and once "withstood him to the face" at Antioch; a party at Corinth claimed his name. Two letters bear his name, and the second calls Paul "our beloved brother".

Acts calls him Silas: a leading man of the Jerusalem church who carried the council's letter to Antioch, then Paul's partner on his second journey. The letters use the Latin form Silvanus (Ramsay notes that "Silvanus is a Latin name"): co-sender of both letters to Thessalonica, a preacher at Corinth, and the man "by" whom 1 Peter was written. 1 Peter gives only the name; it does not say that this Silvanus is Paul's companion, though nothing in it points to anyone else.

John Mark of Jerusalem left Paul and Barnabas at Perga, and Paul's refusal to take him again split the two. Years later he is with Paul, "sister's son to Barnabas", and "profitable to me for the ministry". 1 Peter sends greetings from "Marcus my son", and Papias and Clement of Alexandria, as Eusebius reports, connect Mark with Peter.

Paul's companion from Lystra is co-sender of six letters, Paul's envoy to Corinth, Thessalonica and Philippi, and the recipient of two. He is also the only one of Paul's circle whom Hebrews names: "our brother Timothy is set at liberty".

Galatians names "James the Lord's brother" as a pillar of the Jerusalem church whose envoys could make Peter withdraw from Gentile tables, and 1 Corinthians says the risen Christ "was seen of James". The letter of James is from "James, a servant of God", and Jude calls himself "brother of James". Whether the writer is the same James is an open question, set out on the James, Peter and Jude page.

Galatians names John with James and Cephas as the three who "seemed to be pillars". The three letters of John never give the writer's name (the second and third come from "the elder"), but Irenaeus quotes the first two as written by "John, the disciple of the Lord".

A Levite from Cyprus, Paul's first partner, given "the right hands of fellowship" with him at Jerusalem, later "carried away" at Antioch. Tertullian knew Hebrews as "an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas".

An Alexandrian Jew, "eloquent ... and mighty in the scriptures", who "watered" what Paul planted at Corinth. Luther was the first to suggest him as the writer of Hebrews (Westcott); no ancient writer did (Davidson), and Westcott adds that "there is not the least evidence that Apollos wrote anything".
"Luke, the beloved physician", with Paul in prison and, at the last, "only Luke is with me". Clement of Alexandria, as Eusebius reports, thought Luke translated Hebrews into Greek.

Tentmakers from Rome who taught Apollos and hosted churches in their house; Paul greets them in three letters. In 1900 Harnack proposed Priscilla, with Aquila, as the writer of Hebrews (reported by Dods).

The figure the letters reach for most when they speak of faith. Romans, Galatians and James all quote "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness"; Hebrews makes him the centre of its roll of faith; James and Hebrews both recall his offering of Isaac; 1 Peter holds up Sarah's respect for him.
Named in Romans for the promise of a son, in Hebrews for the faith that let her conceive past age, and in 1 Peter as the model for wives.
"The harlot Rahab" stands in both Hebrews and James for the same act, receiving the spies: Hebrews credits her faith, James says she was "justified by works".

The first murderer is the warning in three groups at once: Abel's sacrifice was "more excellent than Cain" (Hebrews), believers are "not as Cain" (1 John), and the false teachers "have gone in the way of Cain" (Jude).
Hebrews remembers that Enoch "was translated that he should not see death"; Jude quotes a prophecy of "Enoch also, the seventh from Adam", words found in the book of 1 Enoch.
Hebrews praises Noah's faith in building the ark; 1 Peter counts the "eight souls ... saved by water"; 2 Peter calls him "the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness".
Romans quotes Malachi's "Esau have I hated"; Hebrews warns against being "profane ... as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright".
Paul recalls Elijah's complaint that he alone was left; James calls him "a man subject to like passions as we are" whose prayer shut the sky.
Paul sets Adam against Christ ("as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive") and cites the order of creation in 1 Timothy; Jude dates Enoch as "the seventh from Adam".

Paul reads Moses as the giver of the law and contrasts his veiled face with the gospel's open glory; Hebrews calls him "faithful in all his house, as a servant" and lists his faith; Jude tells of the archangel Michael disputing "about the body of Moses".

Paul insists that "a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law", yet that believers are "created ... unto good works"; James that "faith, if it hath not works, is dead"; Hebrews that "without faith it is impossible to please him"; 1 John that "our faith" is "the victory that overcometh the world". Schaff read James's teaching as "no protest against that of Paul, but prior to it"; the James, Peter and Jude page sets out the other readings.

Every group expects its readers to suffer and to hold on: "tribulation worketh patience" (Romans), "the trying of your faith worketh patience" (James), "think it not strange concerning the fiery trial" (1 Peter), "run with patience the race" (Hebrews). Schaff notes that the letters were written "under trial and persecution, some of them from prison, and yet they abound in joy and thanksgiving".

Three letters in two groups quote the same commandment, "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself": Romans and Galatians call it the fulfilling of the law, James "the royal law". 1 Corinthians ranks love ("charity" in the King James) the greatest of faith, hope and charity; 1 John says "God is love"; Hebrews, 1 Peter, 2 John and Jude all make love the mark of the church.

themes.title: Guarding the faith from false teaching

claim.text: From Galatians' "any other gospel" to Jude's "certain men crept in unawares", the letters warn against teachers inside the church: philosophy and vain deceit, "doctrines of devils", "divers and strange doctrines", "damnable heresies", spirits to be tried, and deceivers who deny that "Jesus Christ is come in the flesh". Schaff saw the general letters protesting "against the rising ascetic and Antinomian errors, as Paul does in the Colossians and Pastoral Epistles".

The same Greek word, parousia ("coming, presence"), names Christ's return in 1 Corinthians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, James ("the coming of the Lord draweth nigh"), 2 Peter ("where is the promise of his coming?") and 1 John (counted in the site's Greek text). Deissmann showed it was the everyday word for the state visit of a king or emperor. Hebrews says instead that Christ "shall appear the second time"; Titus and 1 Peter speak of his "appearing" and of "the end of all things".

themes.title: One Scripture, quoted across the groups

claim.text: The groups often quote the same Old Testament verses. "The just shall live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4) appears in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews; Genesis 15:6 in Romans, Galatians and James; "God resisteth the proud" (Proverbs 3:34, in its Greek form) in James and 1 Peter; "Vengeance is mine" (Deuteronomy 32:35) in Romans and Hebrews; the stone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) in Romans and 1 Peter.

themes.title: Leaders and the life of the church

claim.text: Every group assumes a church with leaders: "bishops and deacons" at Philippi, elders appointed "in every city" of Crete, rulers to obey in Hebrews, elders called to pray over the sick in James, elders told to "feed the flock" by Peter, "who am also an elder", and a writer of 2 and 3 John who calls himself simply "the elder", struggling with a local leader who "loveth to have the preeminence".

A church that sent letters by hand depended on open doors. "Given to hospitality" (Romans), "be not forgetful to entertain strangers" (Hebrews), "use hospitality one to another without grudging" (1 Peter), a bishop "given to hospitality" (1 Timothy, Titus), and 3 John's praise of Gaius for sending travelling teachers on their way "after a godly sort".

"This is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians); "holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Hebrews); "be ye holy; for I am holy", quoting Leviticus (1 Peter); "what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation" (2 Peter); "keep himself unspotted from the world" (James); "purifieth himself, even as he is pure" (1 John).

Paul's letters and 1 Peter share a pattern of instructions to wives and husbands, servants and masters, and to subjects of the state: "Wives, submit yourselves" (Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Peter), "servants, be obedient" (Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Timothy, Titus, 1 Peter), "let every soul be subject unto the higher powers" (Romans), "honour the king" (1 Peter).

collection.text: From the first the letters were read aloud and passed on. Paul charges that 1 Thessalonians "be read unto all the holy brethren" and tells Colossae to swap letters with Laodicea; Riggs (ISBE) sees in such reading and exchange the start of the New Testament's growth. Within a generation, Ignatius speaks of Paul's "Epistles" as a set, and Polycarp of Smyrna sends Philippi "the Epistles of Ignatius ... and all the rest which we have by us". 2 Peter already knows "all his epistles" and sets them beside "the other scriptures".

The first collection whose contents we know is Marcion's, about 140: ten letters of Paul, opening with Galatians, without the letters to Timothy and Titus and without Hebrews. The Muratorian list, from Rome late in the second century, counts Paul's church letters as seven, "following the rule of his predecessor John" in Revelation, adds the four personal letters as "hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church", and rejects letters to the Laodiceans and the Alexandrians "forged under the name of Paul".

In the English Bible, which follows the Latin Vulgate (Schaff), Paul's letters to churches come first and his letters to individuals second, and within each set they run from longest to shortest, with one exception: Galatians (2,276 Greek words) is a little shorter than Ephesians (2,478), which follows it. Hebrews (5,052) is longer than every letter except Romans (7,271) and 1 Corinthians (6,972), yet stands after Philemon (343). These counts are from the Greek text the site holds; none of the sources read for this page states the length rule, so it is offered as an observation.

Where Hebrews belonged was settled differently East and West. Athanasius (367) puts it after 2 Thessalonians and before 1 Timothy; Westcott notes that the great Eastern manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and others) and many Greek fathers do the same, while the Western manuscripts place the Pastoral letters straight after Thessalonians, and the old section numbers in Vaticanus hint at a copy with Hebrews after Galatians. The African councils first wrote "of the Apostle Paul, thirteen Epistles, of the same to the Hebrews, one", then simply "the Epistles of Paul, xiv". Luther took Hebrews away from Paul's letters and placed it, with James, Jude and Revelation, at the end of his New Testament (Westcott, Schaff).

The other seven travelled as a group. Eusebius speaks of "the seven so-called catholic epistles", and his translator McGiffert notes that Clement of Alexandria, Origen and Dionysius had used the name before him. Westcott infers, tentatively, from a note in the edition of Euthalius that by the end of the third century the seven had been gathered into one book with Acts. Most ancient manuscripts, versions and lists put them straight after Acts and before Paul, "perhaps as being the works of the older apostles" (Schaff), and Athanasius runs them James, Peter, John, Jude, the same order in which Galatians names the pillars, "James, Cephas, and John"; no source read here says whether that is why. The African canon lists them Peter, John, James, Jude.

Not every letter survived. Paul mentions an earlier letter to Corinth, a letter written "with many tears", and "the epistle from Laodicea". Schaff thought the apostles "probably wrote many more letters than we possess", though "the most important and permanently valuable are preserved".

views.label: Real letters, with literary epistles among them
views.holders: Adolf Deissmann (1895; English 1901 and 1910), from his study of papyrus letters

argument.text: A letter, Deissmann argued, is "a piece of life" meant only for its reader; an epistle is "a product of literary art" in letter form, written for the public. Paul's letters, and 2 and 3 John, are real letters, "raised to the dignity of literature afterwards, when the piety of the churches collected them". James, Peter and Jude, with their undeliverable addresses ("to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad"), are literary epistles; Hebrews is "the earliest example of Christian artistic literature"; 1 John is a "religious diatribe" rather than a letter.

views.label: Real letters, meant from the start to be shared

argument.text: Pratt accepts a line between letter and epistle but finds it too simple: Paul's letters to churches were "as spontaneous and intimately and affectionately personal as the ordinary correspondence" while "intended for general circulation". Schaff calls them pastoral letters, "called forth by special emergencies" yet suited to all: "Tracts for the times, they are tracts for all times." Paul's own orders to read a letter to "all the holy brethren" and pass it to Laodicea point the same way.

questions.question: Why are seven of them called the "catholic" letters?

views.label: Because they are addressed to the church at large
views.holders: Theodoret (5th century, as quoted by Pratt, ISBE); A. C. McGiffert (1890); Philip Schaff (1890); Pratt calls this "now commonly received"

argument.text: "Catholic" meant general or encyclical: the letters are "not addressed to single churches, but generally to the faithful" (Theodoret). James writes to "the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad", 1 Peter to five provinces. Schaff and McGiffert admit the name fits only five of the seven: 2 and 3 John are written to individuals and were classed with 1 John because of their author, while Hebrews, which is just as general, was kept with Paul.

views.label: Because they were universally received
views.holders: A usage of the Western church, which sometimes called them epistolae canonicae (reported by Pratt, ISBE); rejected by McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: Some took "catholic" to mean accepted by the whole church, or "canonical". McGiffert answers that Eusebius uses the name for the very letters he lists as disputed, and that five of the seven were long doubted, so the name cannot have meant "generally accepted".

views.label: Because of their common authorship or their sound teaching
views.holders: Explanations reported without names by Pratt (ISBE), who says only a few support the first

argument.text: Two further readings: that "catholic" marked a shared apostolic authorship, or the orthodoxy of their teaching against heretical letters.

views.label: Because they are literature, not letters

argument.text: For Deissmann the old name says what his study found: "What the Church calls catholic, we require only to call epistle ... catholic means in this connection literary." A letter to "them that are called" everywhere could not be carried by any messenger; it was published, not posted.

questions.question: How were Paul's letters first gathered?

views.label: Gradually, by the churches that kept them

argument.text: The collection "was probably begun not very long after the death of Paul", not all at once (Philemon, he thought, was a late addition), out of "reverential love", on the pattern of the collections made of other famous men's letters.

views.label: From copies kept where the letters were written
views.holders: Adolf Deissmann (Light from the Ancient East, 1910), offered for Romans 16

argument.text: Ancient writers kept letter copy-books, and papyrus fragments of such books survive. Deissmann suggested that Romans 16, which he took for a separate note to Ephesus written down by the same Tertius, ran into Romans in such a copy-book once its heading was lost.

views.label: Already a known set early in the second century
views.holders: J. S. Riggs (ISBE, 1915); the witness of 2 Peter, whose own date is disputed

argument.text: Riggs thinks it "fair to infer that a collection of the Pauline epistles existed" when Polycarp and Ignatius wrote, about 115, and calls Marcion's list (about 140) "the first clear evidence of the canonization of the Pauline epistles". 2 Peter already speaks of "all his epistles"; Zahn dated it about 60-63, Chase about 150.

questions.question: Could a letter be written in an apostle's name by someone else?

argument.text: Deissmann held that many ancient epistles were written under famous names "not by swindlers", a "widespread and unobjectionable literary habit", and he regarded the catholic letters as issued "under a protecting name". Scholars who dated 2 Peter after Peter's lifetime spoke of it plainly as pseudonymous: Mayor wrote of "the pseudonymous writer of 2 P.", and Chase dated it about 150.

views.label: No: the church rejected letters under false names
views.holders: W. G. Moorehead (ISBE, 1915), quoting Marcus Dods; and, from the early church, the Muratorian list and Tertullian

argument.text: Moorehead argued that if 2 Peter were not Peter's "we must pronounce the Epistle a forgery", quoting Dods: "there is no Christian document of value written by a forger who uses the name of an apostle." The early church did reject such writings: the Muratorian list throws out letters "forged under the name of Paul", and Tertullian reports that the presbyter in Asia who wrote a book that went "wrongly" under Paul's name, and confessed he had done it "from love of Paul" was removed from his office. 2 Thessalonians itself warns against a letter "as from us".

views.label: A third way: written by a helper at the apostle's word
views.holders: John Calvin on 2 Peter (1551); Jerome as reported by Mayor and ISBE; Charles Bigg (1901)

argument.text: Calvin thought 2 Peter was set down by "some one of his disciples" at Peter's command; Jerome explained the difference between Peter's two letters by "two different interpreters"; Bigg suggested that if Peter used a secretary for one letter, "this was his rule". 1 Peter itself says it was written "by Silvanus".

views.label: James
views.holders: Philip Schaff (1890); J. B. Mayor (1892) dated it to the 40s

argument.text: Schaff placed James "before A.D. 50" and called it "probably the oldest of the New Testament books"; it "takes no notice of the circumcision controversy" that fills Galatians.

views.label: Galatians
views.holders: John Calvin (1548); some holders of the South Galatian view (reported by Robertson, ISBE)

argument.text: Calvin thought Galatians was written "before that consultation had been held" in Acts 15, since Paul would surely have cited the council's decree; Robertson reports that some South Galatian scholars make it "the very earliest of Paul's Epistles".

views.label: 1 Thessalonians
views.holders: M. G. Easton (1897); George Milligan (1908, reported by Robertson, ISBE)

argument.text: Written from Corinth soon after Timothy returned from Thessalonica: "the first of all Paul's epistles" (Easton).

canon.label: 1 Clement
canon.who: Clement of Rome, writing for the church at Rome to Corinth

claim.text: Clement tells the Corinthians to "take up the epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul" about their parties. Riggs (ISBE) finds that he knows Romans and 1 Corinthians, is much influenced by Hebrews, and echoes 1 Timothy, Titus, 1 Peter and Ephesians. He is silent about 2 Corinthians where he might have used it (Shaw). Echoes are a matter of judgement, and the four group pages list them from their own sources.

canon.label: Ignatius
canon.who: Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to death at Rome

claim.text: Ignatius tells the Ephesians that Paul "in all his Epistles makes mention of you", and echoes 1 Corinthians ("Where is the wise? Where is the disputer?"). Riggs finds language from nearly all of Paul's letters in him, and quotations of 1 Peter and 1 John.

Polycarp quotes Ephesians 4:26 as "these Scriptures", echoes many of Paul's letters, and reminds the Philippians that Paul wrote to them. Eusebius notes that he "made use of certain testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter", and he echoes 1 John's test of confessing "Jesus Christ ... come in the flesh". He also forwards the letters of Ignatius, an early collection in the making.

canon.label: Papias
canon.who: Papias of Hierapolis, as reported by Eusebius

claim.text: Eusebius says Papias "uses testimonies from the first Epistle of John and from that of Peter likewise": the two general letters that were never doubted.

Marcion's "Apostle" held ten letters of Paul, beginning with Galatians and calling Ephesians "to the Laodiceans". He rejected the letters to Timothy and Titus, Hebrews and the catholic letters; Riggs calls his list "the first clear evidence of the canonization of the Pauline epistles".

Irenaeus quotes Paul's letters by name, opens Against Heresies with 1 Timothy's warning against genealogies that "minister questions", quotes 1 and 2 John as written by "John, the disciple of the Lord", and, Eusebius says, takes "many proofs" from 1 John and 1 Peter and mentions Hebrews in a book of discourses.

canon.label: Muratorian list
canon.who: An unknown writer at Rome (the date is debated; usually late second century)

claim.text: The list receives Paul's thirteen letters, Jude and "two belonging to the above-named John", and quotes the opening of 1 John. It does not name Hebrews, James or either letter of Peter.

Clement held Hebrews to be Paul's, written in Hebrew and translated by Luke. Eusebius says his Outlines commented on "Jude and the other catholic epistles"; he quotes Titus, calls 1 John John's "larger Epistle", and comments on 2 John.

Answering Marcion letter by letter, Tertullian defends the letters to Timothy and Titus and insists that Ephesians went to Ephesus. He knows Hebrews as a letter "under the name of Barnabas" and quotes it as weighty, but as from "a comrade of the apostles".

canon.label: Origen
canon.who: Origen of Alexandria, as reported by Eusebius

claim.text: Origen accepts Hebrews ("who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows"), 1 Peter and 1 John; calls a second letter of Peter "doubtful"; says of 2 and 3 John that "not all consider them genuine"; and uses James and Jude.

canon.label: Dionysius of Alexandria
canon.who: Dionysius of Alexandria, as reported by Eusebius

claim.text: Dionysius holds that the Gospel and 1 John share one author, and notes that the "reputed" second and third letters carry not the name John but "the elder".

canon.label: The Syriac Peshitta (date debated)
canon.who: The Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches

claim.text: Both families of Peshitta manuscripts "omit the second and third Epistles of St John, the second Epistle of St Peter, the Epistle of St Jude, and the Apocalypse, but include all the other books" (Westcott). Westcott thought the version very old; it is placed here only for order.

Eusebius sorts the books into "accepted" and "disputed". "Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed", though some reject Hebrews because Rome disputes it; 1 John and 1 Peter are accepted; James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2 and 3 John are "disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many".

A list with exactly the twenty-seven books of today's New Testament (Riggs): the Gospels, Acts, "Epistles (called Catholic), seven", then "fourteen Epistles of Paul", with Hebrews between 2 Thessalonians and 1 Timothy. "Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these."

Jerome records the doubts that remained: many did not count Hebrews as Paul's; some thought James issued by another under his name; many doubted 2 Peter for its style and Jude for quoting Enoch; and "many" gave 2 and 3 John to John the presbyter. Yet he received James, 2 Peter and Jude.

The African canon lists "the Epistles of Paul, xiv", two of Peter, three of John, one of James and one of Jude; its editor notes that it repeats a canon of Hippo (393). The earlier African wording had counted Hebrews apart: "thirteen Epistles, of the same to the Hebrews, one".
